nodes.description: For the intraneural form. Resection aims to remove the tumour, with or without a nerve graft. In a 2021 systematic review, in which 40 of 64 surgically managed cases were resected with or without repair, no lesion recurred after resection (the abstract gives no follow-up after resection). The other sources restrict it. A 30-patient series, in which four patients were completely resected and grafted, advises against complete resection to preserve the nerve's residual function and judges the results of grafting poor, suggesting residual tumour cells as one reason. The longitudinal series warns of further iatrogenic deficit with grafting, as in one of its own patients; it says resection with grafting may be considered for focal, more distal lesions without long-term muscle atrophy when the intra-operative nerve action potential is absent or low, but most of its own cases would not qualify, so it advises that resection should usually not be performed. It found no tumour spreading to initially uninvolved nerves on surveillance MRI, though it recognises that longer follow-up is needed. A 2024 review of childhood cases notes that resection is widely held, though without consensus, to be restricted to shorter lesions; it suggests that complete removal may prevent proximal progression where a terminal branch of a single major nerve is involved over a short length, but advises caution for tumours involving major nerves, and it restates an earlier finding that the tumours only rarely grew in length and did not grow to involve new nerves; a 2026 series, in which the one patient resected and grafted (who had an early severe deficit and also a tendon transfer) illustrates the high morbidity, reserves surgery for select cases, particularly short-segment involvement and rapid progression. Outcomes after resection are mixed. In the 2024 review, of ten patients followed up after grafting, five improved mildly (involved segments of 1.5 to 5 cm) and five, recorded as stable, did not (2.5 to 18 cm, one unknown). Of its nine patients excised without a graft, two were followed up: one without motor improvement and one, asymptomatic before surgery, free of recurrence at 6 years. In the longitudinal series, five patients had resection with grafting: the two who were interviewed, both of whom also had tendon transfers, felt the surgery had improved them (one of them is also one of the review's improved patients), while another's wrist and finger extension worsened after a radial nerve resection and grafting, improving gradually but not to baseline when follow-up ended at 6 months. In the 2024 review's 33 cases with known lesion length, resected lesions were shorter than unresected ones (4.57 against 12.86 cm on average); the review also restates an analysis of 77 surgically treated patients in which the neurological outcome was unchanged in 45.5% and worse in 20.8%, with similar results across operations; the review does not say how the other 34% fared. In a 2016 report, a child excised and grafted had no meaningful recovery of strength at 10 months although the EMG showed reinnervation through the graft; a row of the 2024 review's table matches this child by citation, follow-up and outcome, as the 2.5 cm case among its grafted patients without improvement, and another matches the report's other child, whose two-stage operation included a nerve transfer, as excised, grafted and improved, one of its five improved patients (see the Nerve transfer row). The two reviews pool published cases and may overlap, and the 77-patient analysis may overlap with both. The 2016 authors add, as a general caveat, that features of long-standing neuropathy may reduce the likelihood of reinnervation and recovery. One centre proposes a single operation below 60 years of age for typical cases: excisional biopsy and direct suture for lesions shorter than 5 cm, and a nerve graft, most often with palliative treatment, for longer lesions involving the brachial plexus. In the 2026 series, lesions exceeded 10 cm in 40% and spanned the whole nerve cross-section in 77.8%, which may limit surgical options.

nodes.description: Outside the gut, the soft tissue tumour is a mass of perineurial cells, all positive for epithelial membrane antigen in an 81-case series, from 0.3 to 20 cm across (mean 4.1 cm); a 2012 review says it almost always has no associated nerve. A 1997 report of two cases with a review of the literature describes these tumours as generally small, well circumscribed and not encapsulated; the 2012 review says they are usually well circumscribed and may have a capsule. In the 81-case series nearly all were grossly circumscribed, and 12 had focal infiltrative margins under the microscope. In the gut, where most published cases are colonic, the tumour lies mostly within the mucosa (14% reached the submucosa in the gut-wide review, whose text gives a second split; see the Colonic mucosal polyp row's notes) and usually forms a polyp, though the gastric review's per-case table describes two gastric cases as subepithelial. Epithelial membrane antigen does not stain every gut tumour: among 50 published gut cases stained for it, GLUT-1 and claudin-1, it was positive in 84%, and a review of gastric cases, which shares several published cases with the gut-wide review, found most but not all positive.

Collagen IV was not included in the analysis because such staining was not performed in one of the studies. A chi-square test was used to compare the detection rates of the three markers. The chi-square statistic was 2.52, with a p value of 0.284. These findings indicate that there is no statistically significant difference in the expression of EMA, GLUT-1, or claudin-1 in GI perineuriomas.
